blocks.text: A third-year student pulls the curtain halfway and starts examining an elderly man's abdomen while the ward round is passing. The patient says nothing, but his hands grip the sheet. No harm is done to his abdomen, yet something has been taken from him: his dignity, and his chance to say no.

blocks.markdown: On the ward you are a guest in the patient's most vulnerable moments. Patients and colleagues form judgements about you in seconds, and those judgements affect whether patients agree to be seen, whether staff trust you, and ultimately how much you can learn. This unit covers three habits that underpin professionalism: **introducing yourself properly**, **protecting dignity and privacy**, and **knowing the limits of your role** and when to ask for supervision.

blocks.title: Professionalism
blocks.text: **Professionalism** in medicine is the consistent demonstration of the values, behaviours and relationships that justify the trust patients and the public place in doctors. UK students are held to the same principles of honesty, respect, confidentiality and safety described in the General Medical Council's guidance for medical students, and fitness to practise processes can apply to students.

blocks.markdown:
### Introductions: name and role

Every encounter starts with an introduction. A good introduction (the approach popularised by the *Hello my name is* campaign) includes your **name**, your **role**, what you would like to do, and a request for **permission**. Be honest: do not imply you are a doctor, and do not let others assume so. Wear your identification badge visibly, follow local infection-prevention rules (for example, being 'bare below the elbow' and cleaning hands before and after contact), and introduce yourself to staff as well, so the team knows who you are and who is supervising you.

items: Clean your hands and check the patient's name and identity against their wristband or notes.
Introduce yourself with your name and role: 'Hello Mr Singh, I am Priya Nair, a third-year medical student working with Dr Evans.'
Explain why you are there and what you would like to do, in plain language.
Ask permission and make it clear the patient may say no without it affecting their care.
Check that the patient is comfortable and ready, then proceed.

blocks.title: Introducing yourself and gaining permission
blocks.prompt: You want to take a history from Mrs Davies, an 81-year-old woman in a four-bed bay who was admitted overnight. A nurse is at her bedside. Show how you would introduce yourself to the patient and the nurse, and what you do if she declines.

steps.text: Greet the nurse first if they are with the patient, and give your name, role and the supervising doctor, so the team knows you are present and who to contact.
Clean your hands, ensure your badge is visible, and approach the patient at her level, not standing over her.
Introduce yourself: 'Hello Mrs Davies, I'm Tom Okafor, a third-year medical student. Dr Evans has asked me to talk with you about how you've been feeling. Would that be all right?'
Listen for the answer. If she declines or seems reluctant, accept it, thank her, tell her that her care will not change, and let the supervisor know so that the task can be re-planned.
If she agrees, ask whether she is comfortable, and whether she would like a relative or the curtains closed before you begin.

blocks.answer: A proper introduction states name and role, explains the purpose, and requests permission; a refusal is accepted without pressure and does not alter care.

blocks.markdown:
### Dignity, privacy and confidentiality

**Dignity** means treating patients as individuals with worth, whatever their state of dress or health. **Privacy** is the freedom from unwanted observation or intrusion, and **confidentiality** is the duty not to disclose personal information without a legitimate reason. In practice:

- Close curtains or use a side room, and put up a sign or ask others to wait before examining.
- Expose only the part of the body that needs to be seen, cover it again afterwards, and explain what you are doing.
- Obtain **consent** for each examination, and for intimate examinations offer a **chaperone**; follow the local policy on who can act as one and record it.
- Discuss patient information only where it cannot be overheard: not in corridors, lifts, cafés or social media. Do not use patient-identifiable information on personal devices or in public posts.
- Use the patient's preferred name and be mindful of language, culture and belief.

blocks.caption: Dignity and privacy in practice
rows: Examining the abdomen in a bay
Curtains left open; patient fully exposed
Curtains fully closed, abdomen only exposed, covered afterwards
Discussing results
At the bedside within earshot of other patients
In a private space or with the curtains and a lowered voice, after checking the patient is willing
Intimate examination
Proceeding without offering a chaperone
Explain, obtain consent, offer a chaperone and record it
Sharing cases with friends
Describing an unusual patient in a café
Discussing only anonymised cases in a teaching setting
Photographs
Taking a photo with a personal phone
Never; use only approved clinical photography with consent

blocks.title: Social media and personal devices
blocks.text: Posting about patients, even without names, can identify them and breach confidentiality. Patient information must never appear in personal messaging or social media. If in doubt, leave it out.

blocks.title: Protecting privacy during a conversation
blocks.prompt: You are on a six-bed ward when you are told to explain to Mr Adeyemi, a 59-year-old man, that his bowel investigation will be repeated. He seems embarrassed, and his visitors have just arrived. How do you handle it?

steps.text: Recognise that the content is health information and should not be disclosed in front of visitors unless he agrees.
Ask him quietly whether he would like to talk privately, and offer to move to a side room or ask visitors to step out for a few minutes.
Check that your role allows you to give the information; as a student you should not give news or results yourself, so ask the nurse or doctor to speak to him.
Document that the message was passed on and who spoke with him, and ensure he knows how to ask questions.

blocks.answer: Ask the patient's preference, find a private space, and refer the result discussion to a member of the clinical team, because students should not give results themselves.

blocks.markdown:
### The limits of a student's role

A medical student is a learner. You are not a registered doctor, so you must **not** work beyond your competence or without supervision. In general, as a student you **do not**: prescribe or alter treatment, give test results or prognosis to patients, give a diagnosis as fact, perform invasive procedures unless you have been trained, assessed and are directly supervised, or sign anything that requires a registered clinician (apart from your own signed, countersigned entries where local policy allows). You **do**: observe, take histories and examine under supervision, perform tasks within your assessed competence, and learn.

blocks.caption: When to seek supervision
rows: A patient asks about their diagnosis, prognosis or a result
Be honest that you cannot answer, and ask a clinician to speak with them
A patient looks unwell or their observations worry you
Tell the nurse in charge or your supervisor immediately; do not wait
A senior asks you to do a task you have not been trained for
Say you have not done this before and ask to be supervised or shown first
A patient makes a disclosure, for example about safety or abuse
Do not promise secrecy; explain that you may need to share it and tell your supervisor
You make a mistake or a near miss
Tell your supervisor promptly and honestly so that harm can be prevented
You are unsure of the name or role of the person asking you to do something
Ask for identification and confirm with your supervisor

blocks.title: It is professional to say 'I don't know' and 'I haven't done that before'
blocks.text: Admitting limits is a strength, not a weakness. The unsafe behaviour is carrying on silently beyond your competence, which puts patients at risk and can lead to fitness to practise concerns.

points: Introduce yourself with your name and role, explain what you want to do and ask permission; accept a refusal without pressure.
Protect dignity, privacy and confidentiality by closing curtains, exposing only what is needed, offering a chaperone, and not discussing patients where others can overhear or on social media.
A student must work within their competence under supervision; seek help for questions you cannot answer, concerns about a patient, tasks you are untrained for, and any mistake.

questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate way for a third-year student to introduce themselves to a patient?

options.text: 'Hello Mr Khan, I'm Sam Brown, a medical student working with Dr Patel. Would you mind if I asked you a few questions?'
'Hello, I'm one of the team. I need to take your history.'
'I'm Sam from the doctors. Roll up your sleeve.'
Begin the history without any introduction to save the patient's time.

questions.correctOptionText: 'Hello Mr Khan, I'm Sam Brown, a medical student working with Dr Patel. Would you mind if I asked you a few questions?'

distractorRationale.a: Correct: gives name, role and supervisor, explains purpose and asks permission.
distractorRationale.b: 'One of the team' hides the student role and gives no name.
distractorRationale.c: Implies the person is a doctor and does not ask permission.
distractorRationale.d: Skipping introductions fails basic courtesy and consent.

questions.explanation: A good introduction states name and role honestly, says what you want to do and asks for agreement. Concealing your student status or skipping consent undermines trust.

questions.stem: A patient mistakes you for a junior doctor and asks you whether her scan shows cancer. What is the best response?

options.text: Explain that you are a medical student and cannot discuss results, and offer to ask a member of the clinical team to speak to her
Say you have not seen it but guess it is probably fine
Read the report in the computer system and tell her what it says
Say nothing and walk away

questions.correctOptionText: Explain that you are a medical student and cannot discuss results, and offer to ask a member of the clinical team to speak to her

distractorRationale.a: Correct: corrects the misunderstanding, stays within role and ensures she receives accurate information.
distractorRationale.c: Students should not break bad news or give results; this may be distressing without support.
distractorRationale.d: Ignoring the patient is unprofessional and leaves her worried.

questions.explanation: You should be honest about your role, avoid speculating, and ensure that a suitably trained clinician communicates the result in a suitable setting. This protects both the patient and yourself.

questions.stem: You are about to examine a patient's chest in an open bay. What should you do first to protect dignity and privacy?

options.text: Close the curtains fully, explain the examination, and obtain consent
Ask the patient to undress fully so you can see everything
Proceed quickly so the exposure is short
Ask other patients to look away

questions.correctOptionText: Close the curtains fully, explain the examination, and obtain consent

distractorRationale.a: Correct: privacy, explanation and consent are the foundations of respectful examination.
distractorRationale.b: Full undressing exposes more than necessary.
distractorRationale.c: Speed does not replace consent or privacy.
distractorRationale.d: Asking others to look away does not provide proper privacy.

questions.explanation: Privacy should be established before exposure, and the patient should know what will happen and agree to it. Expose only the area needed and cover it again afterwards.

questions.stem: Two students discuss a patient's diagnosis and name on a crowded hospital lift. Which statement is correct?

options.text: This is a confidentiality breach because others may overhear identifiable information
This is acceptable because they are medical staff
This is acceptable if they speak quietly
This is acceptable if they leave out the date of birth

questions.correctOptionText: This is a confidentiality breach because others may overhear identifiable information

distractorRationale.a: Correct: discussing identifiable patient information in public areas risks disclosure.
distractorRationale.b: Role does not remove the duty of confidentiality in public spaces.
distractorRationale.c: Quiet speech in a lift does not guarantee privacy.
distractorRationale.d: A name and diagnosis are still identifiable.

questions.explanation: Confidential patient information should only be discussed where it cannot be overheard and only with those who need to know. Lifts, corridors and cafes do not meet this standard.

questions.stem: A busy registrar asks you to remove a patient's urinary catheter. You have watched it done but never performed it. What should you do?

options.text: Explain that you have not done it before and ask for supervision or a demonstration first
Do it anyway because refusing would look unhelpful
Ask a more junior student to do it
Agree and then avoid the patient

questions.correctOptionText: Explain that you have not done it before and ask for supervision or a demonstration first

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acting within competence and seeking supervision protects the patient.
distractorRationale.b: Working beyond your competence risks harm.
distractorRationale.c: Passing the task on does not address competence or supervision.
distractorRationale.d: Avoiding the task without saying so leaves the patient's care unresolved.

questions.explanation: Students should only perform procedures when trained, assessed and supervised as required by their school and the ward. Stating the limit openly allows the team to arrange a safe alternative.

questions.stem: While talking to a patient, a student notices the patient's breathing has become noisy and laboured and she is more drowsy than 10 minutes ago. Which is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Immediately alert the nurse in charge or a clinician, stay with the patient, and follow instructions
Finish the history first and then mention it at the end of the shift
Look up possible causes online and wait to see if she improves
Reassure her and leave the bedside to find your supervisor in the morning

questions.correctOptionText: Immediately alert the nurse in charge or a clinician, stay with the patient, and follow instructions

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a deteriorating patient requires prompt help from a qualified clinician.
distractorRationale.c: Searching online wastes time while she is unwell.
distractorRationale.d: Reassurance without escalation leaves a deteriorating patient unattended.

questions.explanation: Recognising that you cannot manage a deteriorating patient on your own is an essential professional judgment. Seeking senior help immediately, and staying with the patient if safe to do so, is the correct action.

questions.stem: True or false: if a patient refuses to be seen by a student, the student should explain the benefits of teaching and encourage the patient to change their mind.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Patients may decline student involvement without it affecting their care, and their choice should be accepted respectfully. Pressuring a patient undermines autonomy and trust.

questions.stem: Describe how you would conduct a respectful examination of a patient's abdomen on an open ward, covering introduction, consent, privacy and dignity.
markingGuide: Cleans hands, introduces self with name and role, and checks patient identity
Explains what the examination involves and why, and obtains consent, making clear the patient may decline
Ensures privacy by drawing the curtains fully or using a side room, and checking no interruption
Positions the patient comfortably, exposes only what is necessary and keeps the rest covered
Offers a chaperone where appropriate and follows local policy
Checks comfort during the examination, thanks the patient and covers them afterwards
Documents or reports findings appropriately to supervisor
questions.explanation: A respectful examination combines honest introduction, informed consent and attention to privacy and exposure. Each step respects the patient's autonomy and dignity and also builds trust.

questions.stem: State five things a medical student should not do on the ward without appropriate supervision or authority, and explain why each limit exists.
markingGuide: Prescribe or change treatment: only registered prescribers may do this and errors could harm
Give test results, diagnoses or prognosis to patients: requires training, accuracy and support, and a student may be misunderstood
Perform invasive procedures without training and direct supervision: risk of harm
Sign entries requiring a registered clinician or present themselves as a doctor: honesty and accountability
Share identifiable patient information outside the clinical team or on social media: confidentiality
Mentions that limits protect patients and that students should say when they have not been trained and seek supervision
questions.explanation: The limits of a student's role exist because patient safety and accountability depend on competence and registration. Naming limits openly, and asking for supervision, is itself professional behaviour.

questions.stem: A patient confides to you that she has stopped taking her medicines because she is afraid of what the doctors will say, and asks you not to tell anyone. What should you do, and why?
markingGuide: Listens respectfully and acknowledges her concern without judgement
Does not promise absolute secrecy because information relevant to her safety must be shared with the clinical team
Explains that you will need to pass the information on to your supervisor or the responsible clinician and why
Tells the supervisor or nurse promptly so the team can discuss it with her sensitively
Recognises that a student does not alter treatment and does not give medical advice beyond their role
Documents or ensures the team documents the conversation appropriately and keeps it confidential otherwise
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is a strong duty, but it is not a promise of secrecy from the care team when safety is involved. Telling the patient honestly what you will share, and with whom, maintains trust and protects her.
